claims.script_text: In 2013, two researchers at the University of Washington split one video game between two buildings. Rajesh Rao got the screen. Andrea Stocco got the space bar.
claims.claim: The demonstration took place in 2013 at the University of Washington, and the two researchers were Rajesh Rao and Andrea Stocco.
claims.evidence: UW News, 27 Aug 2013 (mirrored on ScienceDaily and EurekAlert): Rao, a UW professor of computer science and engineering, partnered with Stocco, a UW research assistant professor in psychology at the Institute for Learning & Brain Sciences. The release text includes the fragment '[Aug.] 12, Rao sat in his lab wearing a cap with electrodes...'. Pilot page (homes.cs.washington.edu/~rao/brain2brain): 'The pilot study involved 2 subjects, both researchers involved in the study (R. Rao as "Sender" and A. Stocco as "Receiver")'. The pilot report is cited as Rao RPN, Stocco A, Prat CS, Bryan M, Sarma D, et al. (2013), 'Direct Brain-to-Brain Communication in Humans: A Pilot Study', 12 August 2013.

claims.script_text: It belongs to a man across campus who can't even see the game. ... split one video game between two buildings. Rajesh Rao got the screen. Andrea Stocco got the space bar.
claims.claim: The two were in separate buildings across campus. Rao saw the game screen, Stocco had the space bar, and Stocco could not see the game.
claims.evidence: UW News 2013: Stocco 'was in his lab across campus wearing a purple swim cap'. The release also says Rao sent a signal to Stocco 'on the other side of the UW campus'. A wire report (East Idaho News) says Stocco 'was in another building'. UW News: 'Stocco, who wore noise-canceling earbuds and wasn't looking at a computer screen, involuntarily moved his right index finger to push the space bar on the keyboard in front of him'. Rao & Stocco in Scientific American: 'Rao alone could see the screen displaying the game. But only Stocco could press the button to fire the cannon.' Pilot page: 'The Sender is unable to press the "fire" button which is only available to Subject 2 (the "Receiver")'. Caveat: no 2013 source found names the two buildings. The ~1 mile distance between buildings in PLoS ONE 2014 refers to the follow-up study.

claims.script_text: Rao's job was to defend a little city. A supply plane flies over? Let it through. A pirate ship launches a rocket? Shoot it down. Easy enough, except the only person who could see the difference had no way to press fire himself.
claims.claim: The game: defend a city, let friendly supply planes through, and shoot down pirate-ship rockets with a cannon, fired with the space bar.
claims.evidence: Rao & Stocco, Scientific American: 'A pirate ship is shooting rockets at a city. The goal is to fire a cannon to intercept each rocket.' CNN, 28 Aug 2013: 'The goal of the game is to hit rockets fired by pirate ships and avoid hitting supply planes.' The pilot session log defines 'Missile' as the pirate rocket and 'Airplane' as the supply plane (experiment page). PLoS ONE 2014: in 50% of trials a friendly 'supply airplane' flew across instead of a rocket, and participants had to avoid firing so the plane could enter the city. Pilot page: the TMS pulse produced an upward hand movement, 'typically resulting in the space bar being hit... and firing the cannon'. Note: the 2014 study replaced the space bar with a touchpad.

claims.script_text: Rao imagines moving his right hand. His real hand stays put. But under that cap, the rhythm of his brain activity changes. A computer is watching for that change.
claims.claim: Rao imagined moving his right hand without moving it, wearing an EEG cap. The computer detected a change in a brain rhythm (mu-band power).
claims.evidence: UW News / Scientific American 2013: 'he imagined moving his right hand (being careful not to actually move his hand), causing a cursor to hit the "fire" button'. UW News: 'Rao sat in his lab wearing a cap with electrodes hooked up to an electroencephalography machine'. Rao & Stocco, Scientific American: 'a tight-fitting cap studded with 32 electrodes'. PLoS ONE 2014 (Rao, Stocco et al.) describes the same system: right-hand motor imagery suppresses mu-band power (the 'mu' rhythm, ~8-12 Hz; subjects' control band reported as 11-13 Hz), and this drop is mapped to upward cursor movement, while no suppression lets the cursor drift down. Caveat: the mu-band detail comes from the 2014 paper, which describes the 2013 pilot as the first demonstration of this BBI. I did not retrieve the pilot page's own wording on mu.

claims.script_text: On his screen, a little cursor climbs. When it hits the target, the computer sends one command over the internet. Fire.
claims.claim: Rao's on-screen cursor moves up to a target at the top of the screen, labelled 'Fire'.
claims.evidence: Pilot experiment page: 'If the cursor hit the blue circular target at the top, the computer decides that the Sender has engaged in motor imagery and sends a stimulation pulse to the Receiver.' PLoS ONE 2014: the Sender guided the cursor 'to either the "Fire" target at the top of the screen or towards the bottom of the screen'; 'When the cursor hit the "Fire" target (a large blue circle) located at the top of the screen...'. Fig. 1 caption: 'The Sender engages in motor imagery to move the white cursor on the left to hit the blue circular target in order to fire the cannon'. UW News 2013: the cursor hit the 'fire' button. Direction is UP (imagery = upward; rest = downward drift). Target: a large blue circle labelled 'Fire'. The cursor starts at the left of its window.

claims.script_text: When it hits the target, the computer sends one command over the internet. Fire.
claims.claim: When the cursor hit the target, a single fire command went over the internet to the other lab's TMS machine.
claims.evidence: Pilot page: 'When the computer detects imagined hand movements, a "fire" command is transmitted over the Internet to the TMS machine, which causes an upward movement of the right hand of the "Receiver."' PLoS ONE 2014: 'When the cursor hit the "Fire" target... the Sender's computer transmitted a signal over the Internet to the Receiver's computer'. That paper puts internet transmission at roughly 10 ms in the 2014 study. The pilot session log shows 'Sending TMS pulse' entries.

claims.script_text: Across campus, a magnetic coil sits over the part of Stocco's brain that helps move his right hand. The command triggers a pulse. His hand jerks up, comes down on the space bar, and the cannon shoots.
claims.claim: A TMS coil sat over Stocco's left motor cortex (right-hand area). The pulse made his hand jerk up and then come down on the space bar.
claims.evidence: Coil placement is confirmed. UW News: Stocco wore 'a magnetic stimulation coil over his left motor cortex, which controls hand movement'. Pilot photo caption: 'Subject 2 (the "Receiver") with TMS coil placed over left motor cortex region and right hand resting slightly above the "fire" key on the keyboard.' Pilot page: the coil 'was localized over the part of the Receiver's brain that controls the wrist and fingers'. The movement is described as upward: the pilot page says the fire command 'causes an upward movement of the right hand of the "Receiver." This usually results in the "fire" key being hit', and the pulse produced 'a muscle twitch and upward hand movement, typically resulting in the space bar being hit'. UW News: he 'involuntarily moved his right index finger to push the space bar'. Fox13: the finger 'involuntarily twitched'. What differs: no source found describes the hand 'coming down' onto the key. Sources say only that the upward twitch usually resulted in the key being hit. It did not always: in Session 4, one stimulation did not cause the fire key to be hit.
claims.suggested_fix: His hand twitches up, hits the space bar, and the cannon shoots.

claims.script_text: and the cannon shoots. The rocket disappears on Rao's screen.
claims.claim: The cannon fired and the rocket was destroyed on Rao's screen.
claims.evidence: Pilot page: the hand movement typically resulted 'in the space bar being hit... firing the cannon' in the Sender's game. PLoS ONE 2014 Fig. 1 caption: fire 'the cannon (bottom center) and destroy the rocket before it reaches the city'. Caveat: a hit was 'typical', not guaranteed. Discover (quoted in secondary coverage) said Stocco's hand would tap the spacebar, '(sometimes) scoring a hit in the game'. The narration describes one successful trial, so it is accurate as written.

claims.script_text: Stocco described the feeling as something like a nervous tic.
claims.claim: Stocco likened the sensation to a nervous tic.
claims.evidence: UW News, 27 Aug 2013 (ScienceDaily mirror), exact wording: 'Stocco compared the feeling of his hand moving involuntarily to that of a nervous tic.' This is the release's paraphrase, not a direct quote, so the narration's unquoted paraphrase is appropriate. Do not put it in quotation marks as Stocco's own words. Rao & Stocco in Scientific American add: 'Stocco did not register the impulse consciously, but his right hand moved anyway.'

claims.script_text: There's a detail I love in the lab notes. Their first session ended early because the network connection failed. Two human brains, ready to go. Bad connection.
claims.claim: The pilot record says the first session was cut short by a network or connection failure.
claims.evidence: The pilot study page (homes.cs.washington.edu/~rao/brain2brain/experiment.html) says: 'Session 1 was terminated early due to network communication issues, which were resolved as the subjects waited for the next session.' The same page reports four experimental sessions of 5-7 trials each, says 'Sessions 2, 3, and 4 witnessed successful transmission of information from the Sender to the Receiver', and says that in Session 4 both achieved near-perfect performance ('Sender: 100% correct detection and transmission of appropriate signal, Receiver: 100% correct elicitation of hand movement upon stimulation; 1 stimulation not causing the "fire" key to be hit'). What differs: (1) this is the public pilot-study web page / report, not 'lab notes'; (2) it says 'network communication issues', not that the connection 'failed'; (3) the issues were fixed while the subjects waited, and the next session went ahead. The core fact (Session 1 ended early because of a network problem) is supported.
claims.suggested_fix: There's a detail I love in their pilot report. Their first session ended early because of network problems.

staging_details: Date and setting: the session ran on 12 Aug 2013 and was announced on 27 Aug 2013. Rao 'sat in his lab'; Stocco 'was in his lab across campus' (UW News 2013). One wire report says Stocco was 'in another building' (East Idaho News).

Rao's headgear: 'a cap with electrodes hooked up to an electroencephalography machine' (UW News 2013). Rao & Stocco in Scientific American: 'a tight-fitting cap studded with 32 electrodes'. For contrast, the 2014 study used a 64-channel Ag/AgCl actiCAP (Brain Products) with g.USBamp amplifiers at 512 Hz (PLoS ONE 2014). Don't apply that spec to 2013.

Stocco's headgear: 'a purple swim cap marked with the stimulation site for the transcranial magnetic stimulation coil', with the coil over his left motor cortex (UW News 2013). Forbes describes the swim cap as serving as the stimulation-site marker.

Coil shape: CIRCULAR, not figure-eight. The pilot page says 'The pulse was delivered though a circle coil at 69% of the machine's power output', from a MagStim Rapid² stimulator. The UW tech report version mentions a 70 mm MagStim circle coil on a Super Rapid² unit. PLoS ONE 2014: 'A 90 mm circular TMS coil was kept in place by an articulated arm.' The figure-eight coil (70 mm Magstim Alpha, over occipital site O1) was used in BrainNet 2019, not here. How the coil was held in 2013 was not confirmed; in 2014 it was held by an articulated arm.

Stocco's hand position: 'right hand resting slightly above the "fire" key on the keyboard' (pilot page photo caption). The pulse produced 'a muscle twitch and upward hand movement' (pilot page). The finger involved was his right index finger (UW News 2013).

What Stocco saw and heard: he 'wore noise-canceling earbuds and wasn't looking at a computer screen' (UW News 2013). The Bottom Line (UCSB) repeats the noise-canceling earbuds detail. 2014 receivers sat in a dark room without seeing the game (Medical Xpress 2014).

Lab coordination: 'The team had a Skype connection set up so the two labs could coordinate, though neither Rao nor Stocco could see the Skype screens' (UW News 2013). Forbes describes it as a Skype connection with no video.

Game layout: a city on the left, attacked by rockets fired from a pirate ship in the lower right; a cannon at the lower/bottom center; in half of the trials a friendly 'supply airplane' flies across instead (PLoS ONE 2014 task description, same game; Fig. 1 caption).

Sender's cursor display: a white cursor starting on the left; a large blue circular 'Fire' target at the top of the screen; imagery moves the cursor up, rest lets it drift down (pilot page; PLoS ONE 2014). The 2014 monitor showed both the cursor window and the game.

Pilot session log on the project page: timestamped lines with trial types 'Missile' (pirate rocket) and 'Airplane' (supply plane), and repeated 'Sending TMS pulse' entries (brain2brain experiment page).

Rao quote usable on screen: 'It was both exciting and eerie to watch an imagined action from my brain get translated into actual action by another brain' (UW News 2013). Coverage also notes Rao was concentrating on the game and at first did not realize it had worked.
Pilot structure: four experimental sessions of 5-7 trials each; Session 1 ended early because of 'network communication issues'; Sessions 2-4 transmitted successfully (brain2brain experiment page).

The 2014 follow-up used a touchpad, not a space bar. PLoS ONE 2014 reports internet transmission of ~10 ms and a mean receiver motor response ~627 ms after the pulse. These are 2014-study figures, retrieved from a search summary only.

claims.evidence: I am upgrading this from the first researcher's 'partly'. A source does describe the hand coming down. Two separate search results quoting the pilot page (homes.cs.washington.edu/~rao/brain2brain/experiment.html) gave the same wording: the stimulation causes 'a quick upward jerk of the Receiver's right hand', and 'this up-down movement of the hand typically (though not always) results in the "fire" key being hit'. The Receiver's right hand was 'resting slightly above the "fire" key on the keyboard'. PLoS ONE 2014 (touchpad version) says the same: because the TMS pulse causes an upward jerk of the hand, the touchpad is actually pressed during the downward part of the movement. On coil placement, UW News 2013 says the coil was 'placed directly over his left motor cortex, which controls hand movement'. Rao & Stocco, Scientific American: 'a TMS coil over his left motor cortex, the brain area that controls the movement of his right hand'. Caveats: (1) the hit was typical, not guaranteed (Session 4 had '1 stimulation not causing the "fire" key to be hit'), but the narration describes one successful trial; (2) UW News says it was specifically his right index finger that pushed the space bar. I could not fetch the pilot page directly, so the 'up-down' wording comes from search-result quotes of it.

staging_details: Date: the pilot ran on 12 August 2013 (the pilot page is dated August 12, 2013, and its session-log entries carry that date). UW announced it on 27 Aug 2013.

Locations, 2013: Rao 'sat in his lab'. Stocco 'was in his lab across campus' (UW News 2013). CNN: 'different parts of the University of Washington's campus'. No 2013 source I found names the buildings. For the 2014 follow-up, UW News 2014 says 'separate buildings on campus about a half mile apart', while the PLoS ONE paper says 'approximately 1 mile apart'. Don't give a distance for 2013.

Rao's setup: 'a cap with electrodes hooked up to an electroencephalography machine' (UW News 2013). Rao & Stocco (Scientific American) describe 'a tight-fitting cap studded with 32 electrodes' (per first researcher; not re-retrieved by me). The trigger signal was 'a drop in the low-frequency oscillations in Rao's brain' (Rao & Stocco, Scientific American). PLoS ONE 2014 gives the mu control band as 11-13 Hz.

Rao's screen: a white cursor starting on the left, plus a blue circular target (Fire). Motor imagery moves the cursor to the target and fires the cannon (PLoS ONE 2014 Fig. 1 caption, same game). The first researcher retrieved 'blue circular target at the top' from the pilot page.

Stocco's setup: 'a purple swim cap marked with the stimulation site for the transcranial magnetic stimulation coil that was placed directly over his left motor cortex' (UW News 2013). He 'wore noise-canceling earbuds and wasn't looking at a computer screen' (UW News 2013). Don't show Stocco watching the game; one secondary summary wrongly says both watched it.

Stocco's hand: the right hand was 'resting slightly above the "fire" key on the keyboard' (pilot page photo caption). The pulse caused 'a quick upward jerk of the Receiver's right hand', and 'this up-down movement of the hand typically (though not always) results in the "fire" key being hit' (pilot page, via search quotes). The finger that pushed the space bar was his right index finger (UW News 2013). So animate a small involuntary lift, then a drop onto the space bar.

Coil shape (from the first researcher; not re-verified by me): a circular coil at 69% of machine output (pilot page), 90 mm circular coil on an articulated arm in 2014 (PLoS ONE). A figure-eight coil belongs to BrainNet 2019, not here.

claims.claim: Three people played a Tetris-like game, each in a separate room.
claims.evidence: Paper (arXiv/bioRxiv text, quoted in search results): 'The three participants in a triad were located in different rooms in the same building on the University of Washington campus and could only communicate with each other through the brain-to-brain interface.' The abstract describes the task as 'a Tetris-like game'. Futurity, reposting the UW News story, says 'three people play a Tetris-like game using a brain-to-brain interface.'

claims.script_text: Two players could see the gap at the bottom. The third could see the block and had to decide whether to rotate it. From that seat, either answer looked reasonable.
claims.claim: Two Senders saw the whole screen, including the gap. The Receiver saw only the block, not the bottom line, and had to decide whether to rotate it (by 180 degrees). Both answers were plausible from the Receiver's view.
claims.evidence: UW News/Futurity: 'Two people, the Senders, can see both the block and the line but can't control the game. The third person, the Receiver, can see only the block but can tell the game whether to rotate the block to successfully complete the line.' Paper: the Receiver 'could only see the block at the top of screen and not the bottom line'. The decision was whether to rotate the piece 180 degrees: 'If the cursor reached the green "Yes" bar, the interface interpreted the participant's decision to be rotation of the block (by 180 degrees).' On 'either answer looked reasonable': no source uses those words, but the design supports it. The paper says that across the sixteen trials 'in half of them the falling block had to be rotated and in the other half, it had to be left in the original orientation', and the Receiver could not see the gap. Rao (quoted in press coverage): Tetris is 'a task where two humans can see the solution but are unable to act, motivating a collaboration with a third human who can act but is unable to see the solution.'

claims.script_text: Each teammate sent a vote.
claims.claim: Each Sender sent a yes/no 'rotate' decision using SSVEP: staring at LEDs that flash at different frequencies.
claims.evidence: Paper (Nature/arXiv): Senders 'convey their decisions of "rotate" or "do not rotate" by controlling a horizontally moving cursor using steady-state visually-evoked potentials (SSVEPs).' They looked at a 17 Hz LED labelled 'Yes' (rotate) or a 15 Hz LED labelled 'No' (do not rotate). In the arXiv v3 and Nature versions the 17 Hz LED is on the left of the screen and the 15 Hz LED on the right. Cursor direction came from comparing EEG power at 17 Hz and 15 Hz, and 'the final decision was made by tallying up the number of epochs in which the greatest power was recorded at either 17 Hz or 15 Hz over a 10-second period.' UW News: 'Beneath the "Yes" option, an LED flashes 17 times per second.' Note that New Atlas and Technology Review reversed the frequency mapping; the paper gives 17 Hz = Yes.

claims.script_text: This time the coil was at the back of the receiver's head, over the part of the brain involved in vision. A little flash in their vision meant "rotate." No flash meant "leave it."
claims.claim: The Receiver's TMS coil was over the occipital (visual) cortex. A phosphene meant 'rotate' and no phosphene meant 'do not rotate'.
claims.evidence: Paper: 'The Senders' decisions are delivered to the Receiver through two TMS pulses delivered sequentially to the occipital cortex, eliciting a phosphene for a "yes" decision or no phosphene for a "no" rotation decision for each Sender.' The abstract describes TMS 'for non-invasively stimulating the visual cortex.' Coil: a 70-mm Figure-8 Alpha coil (Magstim) 'positioned over the left occipital lobe in a location corresponding to site O1 in the 10–20 system' (Nature version). Intensities: 'rotate' was set above the Receiver's phosphene threshold, where a phosphene appeared on 10 consecutive pulses; 'do not rotate' was set below it, where no phosphene appeared on 10 consecutive pulses (arXiv). Narration matches: flash = rotate. Strictly, the coil was slightly left of the midline (site O1), but 'back of the head' is accurate.

claims.script_text: They got one vote from each teammate, chose what to do, then had a second chance to change their answer.
claims.claim: Each trial had two rounds. The Receiver got one TMS signal per Sender and decided. The Senders then saw the result and sent new decisions, and the Receiver could change the decision.
claims.evidence: Paper: the decisions arrive as 'two TMS pulses delivered sequentially', one per Sender. Each pulse lasted 1 ms, with 'an eight-second delay ... enforced between the two pulses to remain within the strictest safety guidelines of TMS stimulation', and 'the Receiver always received the decision from one Sender first, then the other' (arXiv). The Receiver then 'conveyed their decision (rotate or do not rotate) to the game using the same SSVEP-based procedure used by both Senders.' Paper: 'BrainNet's design incorporates a second round of interactions between the Senders and the Receiver, so that the action of the Receiver in the first round can be perceived by the Senders, giving them a second chance to convey (potentially corrective) decisions to the Receiver.' The narration leaves out that the Senders voted again before the Receiver's second decision. It is not wrong, but it can make it sound as though the Receiver reconsidered with no new input.
claims.suggested_fix: Optional, for precision: "They got one vote from each teammate, chose what to do, then got a second round of votes and a chance to change their answer."

claims.script_text: On ten of the sixteen trials, the computer flipped one teammate's advice.
claims.claim: The software made one Sender unreliable by making their transmitted decision wrong in 10 of 16 trials.
claims.evidence: Paper (text quoted in search results): 'our software randomly chooses one Sender to be less reliable by making the decision sent to the Receiver from that Sender incorrect in ten out of sixteen trials.' The arXiv version adds that in each session one Sender was randomly designated the 'Bad' Sender, and that Sender's decision was 'forced to be incorrect, both in the first and second round of each trial' (the 10 of 16 trials). UW News, 1 July 2019: the researchers created a 'bad Sender' by flipping that person's responses in 10 of the 16 trials. 'Computer' fits the paper's 'our software'. One nuance: the paper says the signal was forced to be wrong, which is not quite the same as flipping the Sender's real answer, but UW News itself says 'flipping'.

claims.script_text: Over time, receivers learned whose signal to trust.
claims.claim: Over the course of a session, Receivers learned which Sender was more reliable.
claims.evidence: Abstract: 'Receivers are able to learn which Sender is more reliable based solely on the information transmitted to their brains.' UW News, 1 July 2019: 'Over time, the Receiver switched from being relatively neutral about both Senders to strongly preferring the information from the "good Sender."' Paper: block-by-block regression weights and correlations 'exhibit ascending trends for the "Good" Sender but not the "Bad" Sender'. Mutual information was significantly higher for good Senders (about 0.336) than for bad Senders (about 0.051): t(8) = 5.187, p = .002 in the Nature/arXiv version; the bioRxiv preprint reports t(8) = 4.44.

claims.script_text: Across five teams, they cleared the line about thirteen times out of sixteen.
claims.claim: Five triads averaged 81.25% accuracy, which equals 13 of 16 trials. Accuracy meant a correct block rotation, i.e. a cleared line.
claims.evidence: Abstract: 'Five groups of three subjects successfully used BrainNet to perform the Tetris task, with an average accuracy of 0.813' (81.25%). Scientific Reports: 'The mean accuracy across all triads was 0.8125, corresponding to 13 correct trials out of 16.' Each triad played 16 trials. Accuracy is 'the proportion of correct block rotations achieved by the triad', with chance at 0.5. Performance was above chance: binomial p = 0.002 in one version; the bioRxiv preprint reports t(4) = 7.91, p = .001. A correct rotation is what fills the gap and clears the line, so 'cleared the line' is fair. Two caveats: 13/16 is a mean across triads, not every team's score ('about' covers this), and the search results did not say whether accuracy was scored on the first-round or final decision.
claims.suggested_fix: Optional: "Across five teams, they cleared the line about thirteen times out of sixteen, on average."

claims.script_text: Six years later, a pulse could give you advice. And you could decide the other guy was wrong.
claims.claim: The Receiver chose whether to act, and could go against a Sender's suggestion.
claims.evidence: Paper: the Receiver gets each Sender's decision as a phosphene or no phosphene and 'Receivers made their decision based on whether a phosphene was perceived and conveyed their decision (rotate or do not rotate) to the game using the same SSVEP-based procedure used by both Senders.' The Receiver's choice was their own EEG-controlled action, not triggered by the pulse. When the two Senders' signals conflicted, the Receiver had to choose which to follow. The learning result (C8) shows Receivers came to weight the good Sender over the bad one. IEEE Spectrum: all the receivers noticed the pattern of bad advice and 'chose to listen to the more accurate sender'. 'Decide the other guy was wrong' is an interpretation, but a fair one. Contrast with 2013/2014, where the TMS pulse over motor cortex directly caused the hand movement.

staging_details: Room layout: 'The three participants in a triad were located in different rooms in the same building on the University of Washington campus and could only communicate with each other through the brain-to-brain interface' (BrainNet paper, arXiv/bioRxiv text quoted in search results).
Senders wore EEG caps and could not control the game (UW News 1 July 2019, via Futurity/NeuroscienceNews repost).

Sender screen: the Tetris-like game with a falling block at the top and a partly filled line with a gap at the bottom. Press summaries of Fig. 2 describe a green line at the bottom that the Senders can see and the Receiver cannot (paper Fig. 2 description in search results).

Sender interface: 'Yes' and 'No' on either side of the screen. A 17 Hz flashing LED labelled 'Yes' (rotate) sits on the left and a 15 Hz LED labelled 'No' (do not rotate) on the right (arXiv v3 / Nature version; bioRxiv v2 says only 'opposite sides'). UW News: 'Beneath the "Yes" option, an LED flashes 17 times per second.'

A horizontally moving cursor gives real-time feedback. More 17 Hz EEG power pushes it toward the 'Yes' side. Reaching the green 'Yes' bar means rotate the block 180 degrees; reaching the 'No' bar means keep its orientation. The decision is tallied over a 10-second window (Nature/arXiv).
While the Receiver decides, each Sender's monitor shows a gray background with a text prompt saying the Receiver is deciding (Nature version, per search summary).

Receiver hardware: EEG cap plus a 70-mm Figure-8 Alpha TMS coil (Magstim, UK) driven by a Magstim SuperRapid2 stimulator. The coil sits over the left occipital lobe at site O1 (lower back of the head, just left of center), flush to the head, with the handle parallel to the ground and extending toward the left (Nature version, per search results).

Pulse timing: each Sender's decision arrives as a single 1 ms TMS pulse. Sender 1 and Sender 2 pulses come one after the other, with an eight-second gap for TMS safety. A phosphene (brief flash of light the Receiver perceives) means 'Yes, rotate'; no phosphene means 'No' (arXiv/Nature).

Calibration: each Receiver's phosphene threshold was measured first (PEST method). The 'Yes' intensity was raised in 5% steps until a phosphene appeared on 10 consecutive pulses. The 'No' intensity was lowered in 5% steps until no phosphene appeared on 10 consecutive pulses (arXiv).

Receiver screen: shows the falling block at the top but not the bottom line/gap. In paper Fig. 2 ('Examples of Screens seen by the Receiver and the Senders across Two Rounds'), the Receiver's screens are in the left column and the Senders' in the right column.
Receiver decision: made with the same SSVEP LED/cursor interface as the Senders (17 Hz Yes / 15 Hz No), so the Receiver also stares at flashing LEDs to answer (Nature/arXiv; CACM).
Round 2: after the Receiver's first decision, the Senders see the block, possibly now rotated, mid-way through its fall, and send a second (possibly corrective) decision (Nature, per search results).

Session design: 16 trials per triad. Half needed a rotation and half did not. One randomly chosen Sender per session was the 'Bad' Sender, whose transmitted decision was wrong in 10 of 16 trials, in both rounds (arXiv / UW News).
Press photo: Futurity's repost of the UW story shows a researcher fitting the TMS coil and EEG cap on a Receiver (search-result description; image not viewed directly).
Press inconsistency to avoid: New Atlas and MIT Technology Review reversed the LED mapping (15 Hz = rotate). The paper says 17 Hz = Yes/rotate.

claims.script_text: He moved someone else’s finger with his mind.
claims.claim: Rao's EEG-decoded motor imagery triggered a TMS pulse that made Stocco's finger/hand move, so it is fair to say he moved someone else's finger with his mind.
claims.evidence: The movement is confirmed. UW News (27 Aug 2013, washington.edu/news/2013/08/27/...) says: 'Using electrical brain recordings and a form of magnetic stimulation, Rajesh Rao sent a brain signal to Andrea Stocco on the other side of the UW campus, causing Stocco's finger to move on a keyboard.' A UW photo caption adds: 'Stocco's right index finger moved involuntarily to hit the "fire" button.' The mechanism is confirmed by the Brain2Brain experiment page (homes.cs.washington.edu/~rao/brain2brain/experiment.html, read through search excerpts because the host is blocked): the sender 'imagined moving the right hand', the computer recognised that imagery and turned it into a magnetic pulse to the receiver's left motor cortex, and the resulting hand movement 'typically (though not always)' hit the fire key. The researchers' own caveats: Rao 'cautioned this technology only reads certain kinds of simple brain signals, not a person's thoughts' (UW News).
